concept.name: Quote stuffing
concept.definition: A disruptive order-book practice in which a trader rapidly submits and cancels very large numbers of bids or offers to overload a trading venue's quotation system, delay other participants' market data or executions, or create misleading impressions of market activity. The CFTC has described submitting or cancelling bids or offers to overload a registered entity's quotation system as conduct 'of the character of' spoofing, which Dodd-Frank made unlawful as a disruptive practice under CEA section 4c(a)(5).
concept.intuition: Imagine shouting thousands of fake orders into a market every second and instantly retracting them, just so everyone else's screens and systems choke on the noise while you exploit the confusion.
concept.mechanics: An algorithm floods the order book with quotes that are cancelled within milliseconds, inflating message traffic and quote-to-trade ratios. The burst can slow data feeds and matching engines, widen apparent depth, and obscure the true book, giving the stuffer a latency or informational edge over slower participants.
concept.failure_modes: High message rates also arise from legitimate market making and aggressive re-quoting in volatile markets, so detection based purely on quote-to-trade ratios produces false positives; the prohibited element is the disruptive intent or effect, not speed itself.
concept.misconceptions: It is not simply 'posting many quotes' — high quote traffic from bona fide market makers is lawful; quote stuffing specifically involves orders not intended to trade, used to jam or mislead the market.
concept.example: An HFT firm fires 5,000 orders per second into an equity's book and cancels 99.9% of them within 10 milliseconds, causing consolidated-feed latency that slows rival algorithms while the firm trades on the faster direct feed.

citations.source: CFTC, Antidisruptive Practices Authority (Interpretive Guidance), 78 FR 31890
citations.section: Discussion of CEA section 4c(a)(5)(C) and proposed spoofing description (footnote 25)
